en: The first is that the contract authorizes the change. It is true that the terms normalize mutability and stabilize the scenario, by treating content as a revocable license and allowing alterations, but abusive teleology is not reducible to the contract, and contractual elasticity does not solve the problem when the offer incorporated the attribute into the core of the good. Private autonomy, moreover, does not authorize organizing enjoyment on bases structurally incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability. The second is that nothing was false, the text is not scandalous and the service remains available. The answer is that the CDC requires neither literal falsity nor scandalous text in order to react.
The supplier's private autonomy does not authorize the organization of enjoyment on bases structurally incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability.<1>p. 665</1>

Thus, although abusive teleology is not reducible to the contract, the contract contributes to stabilizing the scenario in which the platform reorganizes by design the form of access and enjoyment, shifting the consumer onto tracks of consumption and permanence that primarily serve the supplier's rationality <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 451</3>
The CDC need not wait for a scandalous text in order to react.<1>p. 668</1>

The third is that of moralism or judicial impressionism. The answer is that the category is a technique of containment, because it only makes sense with a demonstrated pattern and a cumulative test, and because it refuses moral judgment about technology. The fourth is that heterogeneous facts are being artificially added together. With Ferraz Jr., the answer is that dogmatics brings functionally similar occurrences back to a unitary framework, treating phenomena as normed sets and forming standards by the principle of similarity. The fifth is that the consumer cannot demonstrate anything without knowing the internal data, and here the answer returns to decidability, since the qualification does not depend on knowing all the data from the outset, and the signs of proof for each family are largely in plain view.

Dogmatics does not operate by infinite reproduction of the empirical, but by bringing functionally similar occurrences back to a unitary normative framework, capable of guiding decision and legal consequence <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 99; p. 312-313])</2>.<3>p. 666</3>

Abusive teleology does not derive from an artificial aggregation of heterogeneous facts, but from the functional similarity between occurrences that reveal a common rationality of exploitation.<1>p. 667</1>
For this reason, the expectation that qualification depends on knowing all the relevant data from the outset becomes inadequate, as already established.<1>p. 447</1>
What does the category not reach?

It does not name every bad experience, every consumption frustration or every unfavorable change, and the unlawful act does not arise from a single episode that can be treated as an accident. It does not apply to design as style or interface aesthetics, nor does it prohibit changes, technical evolution or internal rebalancing. The qualification depends on the structure of the case, and not every dispute reveals a defect of regime.
It does not name every bad experience, every consumption frustration or every unfavorable change made on a platform.<1>p. 669</1>

What is called into question is not design as style, visual language or interface aesthetics, but the incorporation, into the regime of provision, of a stable, verifiable exploitative purpose functionally oriented toward producing asymmetries.<1>p. 664</1>
This is not an effort to prohibit changes, technical evolution or the necessary internal rebalancing of digital systems.<1>p. 393</1>

Aesthetic alteration calls for a reconciliation that falls to the interpreter. As a rule, predominantly aesthetic changes fall outside the concept of IOC, unless they form a convergent set of signs of an unlawful act of architecture, and a mere preference for an old experience is not equivalence. At the same time, visual experience and distinction may be part of the core that motivated the purchase of a cosmetic, as the case of visual effects updates to old cosmetics shows, discussed in the chapter on equivalence. The line runs through what was sold. What counts is what the offer incorporated into the core of the utility, and not the consumer's attachment.

The category also has a definite place in the sequence. It comes after the object is qualified, the vulnerability identified, information and advertising assessed, auditability required and equivalence tested, and so it works as the closing category of the regime of controllability, because it answers whether the environment reveals legitimate governance or a program of exploitation. Proof and restoration come next, and restoration also performs a closing function in the regime, because it answers what to do with the conflict. The two statements deal with different questions, which the chapters on proof and on remedies develop. Asserting the unlawful act, in any case, depends on chained demonstration, and nothing in the test guarantees the outcome of a claim.
For this reason, abusive teleology works as the closing category of the regime of controllability.<1>p. 734</1>

Once the object is qualified, the vulnerability identified, the duties of information and advertising assessed, auditability required and functional equivalence tested, it becomes possible to ask whether the environment as a whole reveals only legitimate governance or already operates as a program of exploitation incorporated into enjoyment itself.<1>p. 734</1>
It is this requirement of chaining that prevents the trivialization of the category and preserves its institutional usefulness.<1>p. 734</1>

The jurist's way through the regime of digital consumption · Lex Plataformae
The jurist's way

This way reconstructs, for lawyers, judges, members of the Public Prosecutor's Office and students, the legal regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption. Each chapter starts from a problem, shows why the ordinary reading is not enough and arrives at what can be demonstrated and requested.
What are the chapters?
<1>How to read this doctrine</1>
<1>Why technique changes the legal question</1>

The defense that the loss was just the way the software works treats as nature what, in a governed digital environment, is a design choice made by someone. The philosophy of technique, of media and of design brings these choices back to the field of imputation, and each of its authors changes the question the jurist puts to the case.
<1>How the platform extracts value</1>
<1>The Immaterial Object of Consumption</1>

The Immaterial Object of Consumption is the category that qualifies as an immaterial product, under Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, the utility that exists only as a position of enjoyment sustained by private governance. Without this qualification, the case seems to have no object, and with it the jurist knows what to demonstrate in court.
<1>The law of the platform</1>

The law of the platform is the private ordering by which the platform creates rules, converts them into architecture and enforces them through sanctions that reach the consumer's position of enjoyment, without being state law or a mere contract. This order is formed and punishes by design, reaches a consumer who lives inside it and finds its limit in state law.
<1>Semiotic vulnerability</1>

Semiotic vulnerability is the form the consumer's factual vulnerability takes when the platform controls the signs, metrics, visibility and records through which the consumer understands what was acquired, perceives what was lost and tries to prove the loss. In these environments formally informed consent is not enough, and the category fits into Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> without creating a new vulnerability.
<1>Information, advertising and anticipation</1>

On platforms, the decision to buy is formed in an environment in which information, advertising, calendar and signs of prestige operate together, and the value of what is bought depends on criteria the supplier itself administers. For this reason the duty to inform is read as verifiable adequacy, the offer as controllable management of meaning, and the defense that everything was in the accepted terms loses force.
<1>Open auditability</1>
<1>Functional value equivalence</1>

Functional value equivalence is the criterion that judges whether the alteration of an Immaterial Object of Consumption preserved, in substantial terms, what justified the acquisition. The test rests on Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, reaches the appearance of an item when that is what was bought and leads to restoration.
<1>Abusive teleology and the unlawful act of architecture</1>
<1>The protected goods</1>
<1>The constitutional order and the sectoral framework</1>

Platform governance is an exercise of private economic power over positions of continued enjoyment, and the jurist needs to know on what basis the legal order limits it without treating the company as the State or reducing the conflict to the contract. This basis comes from the economic Constitution, from the horizontal effect of fundamental rights and from the CDC, and the Legal Framework for Electronic Games and the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents help to see the sector without resolving the conflict of enjoyment on their own.
<1>Intellectual property</1>

Intellectual property enters the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption as part of the infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, maintained, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested, and not as a topic parallel or superior to consumer protection. Exclusivity has come to organize competition and enjoyment, and the social function, read from Article 5, item XXIX, of the Federal Constitution<1><2>4</2></1>, makes it a field of reconciliation with the CDC.
<1>Proof</1>

In platform-governed consumption, the disputed fact arises and remains within the supplier's infrastructure, so that whoever controls records, versions and traces of sanction also controls the conditions for reconstructing what happened. Semiotic vulnerability then turns into allegation, proof and request, and the CDC and the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) provide the instruments to request the right record and allocate the burden.
<1>Remedies</1>

Remedies close the examination of a conflict over an Immaterial Object of Consumption, because they answer what to do with the injury once the object is qualified, the change reconstructed, the equivalence assessed and the proof organized. Primacy belongs to functional restoration and regime correction, and compensation comes after them, not in their place.

Information, advertising and anticipation
Why is examining the clause, the notice and the ad separately not enough?

The traditional examination asks, separately, whether the clause existed, whether the information was technically available and whether the advertising piece contained literal falsity. On platforms, information, advertising and abusive practices operate jointly in forming expectation, urgency, trust and tolerance for frustration, so that the object of control becomes the integrated decision-making arrangement through which the platform organizes the consumer's adhesion and permanence, distributing visibility, scarcity, comparability and promise of value. Sensitivity is greater in the Immaterial Object of Consumption, because the decision concerns a governed future experience, continuously modulated by architecture, curation and private sanction, and the initial expectation becomes part of the very legal substance of enjoyment.
In contexts under hypercuratorial anticipation, information, advertising and abusive practices belong to the same dogmatic problem.<1>p. 634</1>

In platform contexts, information, advertising and abusive practices cannot be examined as autonomous phenomena, isolated in watertight compartments, because, in the real process of consumption, they operate jointly in forming expectation, urgency, trust and tolerance for frustration. The legal problem is no longer exhausted in knowing whether a given clause existed, whether certain information was technically available or whether an advertising piece contained literal falsity.<1>p. 629</1>

What needs to be controlled is the integrated decision-making arrangement through which the platform organizes the consumer's adhesion to and permanence in the ecosystem, distributing visibility, scarcity, comparability and promise of value in a way functional to its own interests.<1>p. 629-630</1>

The consumer's decision concerns a governed future experience, continuously modulated by architecture, curation and enforcement, so that the initial expectation becomes part of the very legal substance of enjoyment.<1>p. 630</1>

The shift is one of method. Information is no longer read only as declaratory content, advertising is no longer promotional decoration and the abusive practice is no longer a marginal event after the contract. Claudia Lima Marques traces the mandate of transparency back to the search for the consumer's true and free will, as a precondition for the consumer to realize legitimate expectations, and it follows that transparency must run through the entire process of approaching the object, from capturing attention to settling expectation. The lawfulness of the relationship, therefore, is assessed by the set of pre-contractual and contextual manifestations that shaped will and the perception of risk, and not only by the final text of the bond.

Information cannot be read only as declaratory content; advertising cannot be treated as promotional decoration; and the abusive practice cannot be reduced to a marginal event after the contract.<1>p. 630</1>

The meaning of the mandate of transparency can be traced back to the search for the “true and free will of the consumer”, functioning as a “precondition” for the consumer to freely express their will and realize their legitimate expectations, that is, those that led them, “duly informed about the product or service, aware of their future contractual rights and duties”, to choose a given supplier as contractual partner <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 818-819)</2>.<3>p. 630</3>

Transparency, in this framework, is not a mere formal requirement of the final moment of contracting, but a presupposition that must run through the entire process of the consumer's approach to the object, from the capture of their attention to the settling of their expectation as to what will be obtained, lost or tolerated as admissible frustration. For this reason, the lawfulness of the relationship cannot be assessed only by the final text of the bond, but by the set of pre-contractual and contextual manifestations that shaped the consumer's will and perception of risk.<1>p. 630</1>

When the value of the object depends on administered visibility, symbolic equivalences and time governed as a program, the central problem is no longer just the content of the item and becomes the demonstrability of the link between promise and enjoyment. Three descriptions support this diagnosis, that of the spectacle, that of the simulacrum and that of the curated promise, and each of them identifies, for the jurist, a form of asymmetry of verifiability.
The contribution of the spectacle to the legal question, at this point, is not to offer a moral critique of media, but to delimit a specific form of asymmetry of verifiability.<1>p. 294</1>
The result is an asymmetry of verifiability, which makes it plausible to operate equivalence by appearance as practical shielding against the demonstration of nonperformance.<1>p. 313</1>
What does the society of the spectacle change for the jurist?

Guy Debord makes it possible to shift the focus from the sign to the environment, because on platforms the promise does not circulate only as meaning, but as scene. Spectacle, in this reading, does not designate media excess, but the social relation between people mediated by images that Debord describes, a form of mediation that reorganizes experience under a logic of visibility. The platform institutes a regime of legibility in which positions become public through selection, ordering and highlighting, and the offer no longer presents itself as an isolated property of an item but as access to a position, whose relevance depends on how the environment produces visibility and comparison. For this reason social proof is part of delivery itself.
The next step consists in shifting the focus from the sign to the environment, because, on platforms, the promise does not circulate only as meaning, but as scene.<1>p. 281</1>

Here, spectacle does not designate media excess nor a mere addition of images to the real, but a social form of mediation in which relations operate through representations and reorganize experience under a logic of visibility. Debord formulates this perspective when he states that the spectacle is not a collection of images, but a social relation between people mediated by images <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, [p. 26])</2>.<3>p. 282</3>

The platform institutes a regime of legibility in which positions are made public through selection, ordering and highlighting, causing differences to acquire economic value because they become measurable in displayed hierarchies. Thus, the offer of the IOC does not present itself as an isolated property of an item, but as access to a position whose relevance depends on how the environment produces visibility and provides parameters of comparison.<1>p. 283</1>

The acquired position of enjoyment only fully fulfills its economic function when it can be perceived, compared and validated in a public circuit, so that social proof is part of delivery itself.<1>p. 284</1>

Gamification operates, in this framework, as a discipline of the present, because remaining comes to mean staying measurable and recognizable on a scale updated in real time. In the ranking system of League of Legends, official support describes tiers and divisions with the risk of regression, a daily penalty of 75 league points for inactivity at the highest levels and the acknowledgment that most of these players play practically every day to keep their position. The company itself recalibrates the signs of prestige, as when it removed the protection against demotion between divisions. And the displayed position is not stable property, because it exists while the access bond remains operative, and the Terms of Service treat use as a limited and revocable license, automatically canceled when the account is closed. Rank, honor and reputation thus behave as attributes of an administered position.
The stability of prestige, here, is not rest, but vigilance.<1>p. 286</1>

When comparison is organized as an administered hierarchy, visibility takes the form of a socially naturalized system of measurement. Everyday life comes to be governed by continuous progressions and repositionings, in which remaining is not only continuing to use, but staying measurable and recognizable on a scale updated in real time. Gamification, here, operates as a discipline of the present.<1>p. 284</1>

In explaining how ranked games work, official support formalizes the existence of tiers and divisions as a general structure of progression, indicating that moving from one level to another presupposes completing internal stages and admits the risk of regression <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026j)</2>.<3>p. 285</3>

The document not only acknowledges decay due to inactivity, but also makes its intensity explicit, stating that there is a “daily penalty of 75 LP against inactivity” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026g)</2>.<3>p. 286</3>

Official support describes a daily decay due to inactivity and even acknowledges that this leads most top players to play practically every day to keep their position <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026g)</2>.<3>p. 286</3>

The company itself recalibrates the signs of prestige and reconfigures the filters of frustration and reward to keep the circuit “fun and rewarding”, which includes modifying demotions and removing protections that softened the fall between divisions, making the transition more “fluid” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024f)</2>.<3>p. 286</3>

The dogmatic tie of this device is that the displayed position, with its emblems, divisions and places in rankings, does not constitute stable property of the consumer. It exists while the legal bond of access remains operative.<1>p. 286-287</1>

In the Terms of Service, use of the services and of virtual content is granted by a limited and revocable license, conditioned on compliance with the contract, and closing the account automatically cancels the license <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 287</3>
The result is that rank, honor and reputation behave as attributes of an administered position. They depend on the service, the registration and the rules in operation.<1>p. 287</1>

Urgency, in this regime, is not spontaneous emotion nor a subjective reaction to a promotion, but an effect of the governance of time and visibility, of an environment that organizes opportunities as windows and treats relevance as something that expires. Trust also changes address, because the consumer's security tends to shift from the item to the environment that makes it operative, and that same environment controls the criteria of relevance and can recalibrate value without explicitly breaking the minimum delivery of the item. The legal consequence is that the relevant asymmetry is not reducible to a deficit of contractual information, because the correspondence between promise and experience depends on curations, orderings and scripts of recognition that can be recalibrated without clear announcement and without ostensible alteration of the item. The spectacle matters, therefore, as a material layer of the evidentiary problem, since it describes how the evidence of what has value can be administered and naturalized as an objective datum of the environment.

Urgency, in this regime, is not spontaneous emotion nor a simple subjective reaction to a “promotion”. It is an effect of the governance of time and visibility, that is, of an environment that organizes opportunities as windows and treats relevance as something that expires.<1>p. 290</1>

Since enjoyment of the IOC depends on visibility, comparison and validation in a public circuit, the consumer's security tends to shift from the item to the environment that makes it operative, that is, to the stability of the signs, hierarchies and scripts through which that good “has value” socially. The platform thus comes to function as a source of informal institutional trust, because it appears as the guarantor of the continuity of the game of recognition in which reputation, belonging and prestige remain legible and updated. This trust is exploitable by continuous governance, since the same environment that offers confirmation also controls the criteria of relevance and the parameters of repositioning, and can recalibrate value without explicitly breaking the minimum delivery of the item.<1>p. 291</1>

If the value of the IOC depends on visibility, comparison and validation, and if this regime presents itself as natural evidence of the environment, the relevant asymmetry cannot be reduced to a deficit of contractual information.<1>p. 292</1>

Under these conditions, the consumer faces not only opacity about clauses, but a practical limitation of verification, since the correspondence between promise and experience depends on curations, orderings, cuts of visibility and scripts of recognition that can be recalibrated without clear announcement and without ostensible alteration of the item.<1>p. 292</1>

The dispute no longer revolves only around the isolated item and comes to involve the regime of visibility that makes the acquired position comparable and confirmable, because alterations in this regime can lower, raise or neutralize a promise without producing an unequivocal technical event of rupture. For this reason, the spectacle matters as a material layer of the evidentiary problem, since it describes how the evidence of what has value can be administered and naturalized as if it were an objective datum of the environment.<1>p. 295</1>
How does the simulacrum shift the proof of delivery?

Jean Baudrillard provides the distinction between feigning and simulating. Feigning preserves the reality principle, while simulation throws into crisis the boundary between true and false, and the simulacrum describes a functioning in which sign equivalence is enough to keep value circulating and the promise seeming fulfilled. The analytical gain is to separate the public continuity of value from the effective continuity of the purchased experience, which makes it possible to describe capture without calling it a lie, as the administration of criteria of equivalence capable of concealing relevant losses without ostensible rupture of the object. Sign value can thus be treated as an economic dimension proper to consumption. As Baudrillard recalls, one never consumes the object in itself, because objects are manipulated as signs that distinguish. The signs of delivery on platforms are novelty, rarity, exclusivity, prestige, belonging, distinction and edition, classificatory categories that organize hierarchy and comparison in real time.

The difference is structural, because feigning preserves the reality principle, while simulation throws into crisis the boundaries between true and false, real and imaginary <1>Baudrillard</1><2>(Baudrillard, 1991, [p. 9-10])</2>.<3>p. 295-296</3>
Here, simulacrum describes a functioning in which sign equivalence is enough to keep value circulating and the promise seeming fulfilled.<1>p. 296</1>

The analytical gain is to separate the public continuity of value from the effective continuity of the purchased experience, making it possible to describe capture not as a “lie”, but as the administration of criteria of equivalence that operate on the symbolic plane and can conceal relevant losses without ostensible rupture of the object. With this, sign value can be treated as an economic dimension proper to consumption, and not as a mere by-product.<1>p. 296</1>

The starting point is the rejection of consumption as appropriation of use value, since “one never consumes the object in itself” and objects “are always manipulated as signs that distinguish the individual”, whether by affiliation to the reference group or by demarcation from a higher status <1>Baudrillard</1><2>(Baudrillard, 1995, p. 60)</2>.<3>p. 297</3>

Novelty, rarity, exclusivity, prestige, belonging, distinction and “edition” are not communicational adornments. They are classificatory categories that define what should be read as superior, desirable and “of the moment”, organizing hierarchy and comparison in real time.<1>p. 297-298</1>

The mechanism appears when the environment reorders categories and signs without this emerging as rupture, and restoration takes the form of nominal equivalence, preserving the item's name, class, label, displayable position and internal commensurability while restrictions, effects, access, relevant uses or performance conditions are altered. It appears in the champions of League of Legends, who are not an automatically available roster, because they circulate as store assets. Riot Games publicly stated that Aatrox needed to be rethought from scratch, which amounts to a complete overhaul packaged as continuity. In the case of Mordekaiser, shifted to the dynamics of the duo lane, the change compares to that of an outside hitter converted into a libero in volleyball, who stays on the roster and with the same name on the scoresheet while the practice that justified the investment is replaced. The analogy does not suggest another game, because the sport remains and what changes is the function.

Since the renewal of distinctive material and obsolescence operate as engines of the system, the environment can shift categories, reorder relevances and recalibrate signs without this appearing as rupture, because what is maintained as “proof” is the persistence of the circuit of recognition. In this condition, restoration may take the form of nominal equivalence, preserving the item's name, class, label, displayable position and internal commensurability, while restrictions, effects, access, relevant uses or performance conditions that constituted the acquired position of enjoyment are altered.<1>p. 304</1>

The sign remains identifiable, remains counted and remains displayable, since the name, the presence in the account and the public frame of belonging are not removed. Except that here a “champion” is not a character automatically available like the roster of a classic game. It circulates as a store asset, displayed and purchasable within the client itself, and its presence in the account functions as a public sign of collection and belonging.<1>p. 305</1>

Riot itself, in a public text, states that the changes would be “the biggest” ever made at the gameplay level and that Aatrox “need[ed] to be rethought from scratch” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2018c)</2><3>p. 306</3>
This is not fine-tuning. It is a complete overhaul, but packaged as continuity, since the public sign remains and social equivalence reorganizes around it.<1>p. 306</1>

The case of the champion Mordekaiser, in the rework that pushed him into the dynamics of the duo lane, is even more radical because the nominal restoration is not limited to swapping the functional content of the “same” champion.<1>p. 306</1>

It is the difference between having an outside hitter, whose excellence is measured by jump, ball timing, variety of attack and the ability to decide the point under the block, and, by unilateral decision of the team's internal rules, seeing that athlete converted into a libero, whose excellence is measured by defensive reading, short movement, forearm pass control, coverage and stability of reception. The athlete remains on the roster, remains “the same name” on the scoresheet, remains in uniform and present on court, but the practice that justified the investment and that defined the technical pleasure of enjoyment was replaced by another form of participation.<1>p. 306</1>

The volleyball analogy does not intend to suggest that it is “another game”, but precisely the opposite: it preserves the crucial point that the sport remains the same, while the function and the regime of participation are replaced.<1>p. 306</1>

The consequence for the offer is direct. It materially includes the form of recognition of the good in the ecosystem, and for this reason a reading of adequacy that treats the good as a closed unit and measures performance by what remains technically accessible tends to miss the object. When restoration preserves only the name or the appearance, the consumer still faces a compatible sign, but may lose what was part of their legitimate qualitative expectation, to the point that the decision to contract might not have occurred had the alteration been present from the start. The link between promise and enjoyment tends to be replaced by a link between promise and sign, and for this reason legally adequate restoration must be read as substantive restoration of the position of enjoyment, and not as nominal or imagistic equivalence.

The offer, in these markets, materially includes the form of recognition of the good in the ecosystem, since it is this public legibility that stabilizes commensurability and makes the promise operate as “delivery” for the consumer and for the community. For this reason, a legal reading of adequacy that treats the good as a closed unit and assesses performance only by what remains technically accessible tends to miss the object, because it ignores the semiotic dimension that is part of the acquired position of enjoyment itself.<1>p. 308</1>

For this reason, restorations that preserve only the name or the appearance can keep the code running and, even so, destroy the position of enjoyment that gave the good meaning and value. In these cases, the consumer still faces a “compatible” sign, but loses, in practice, what was part of their legitimate qualitative expectation about what was acquired, to the point that the decision to contract might not have occurred had this alteration been present from the start.<1>p. 309</1>

In this condition, trust becomes exploitable by continuous governance, because the platform can recalibrate the bases of the experience from within and, even so, maintain the appearance of performance through the visible stability of the code, which makes it difficult to turn a relevant loss into a demonstrable rupture. This makes the core of the evidentiary problem clearer: the promise-enjoyment link tends to be replaced, in practice, by a promise-sign link, and it is this shift that makes auditability and functional value equivalence necessary responses of verifiability, and not moralism against the symbolic.<1>p. 310</1>

The consequence is objectively identifiable, since legally adequate restoration must be read as substantive restoration of the position of enjoyment and not as merely nominal or imagistic equivalence, since equivalence by appearance is precisely the space in which the simulacrum makes it possible to keep the economic circuit running without preserving what was actually acquired.<1>p. 311</1>
What does the Exalted tier show about price, rarity and random draws?

After the public controversy over the meaning of the Ultimate category, Riot Games created the Exalted tier and the Sanctum, presented as a shelf above the traditional top of the catalog. The chapter on abusive teleology examines the purchase path, and here what matters is the promise. The material grammar of the Exalted skins largely recapitulates that of the Ultimates, with transformation, multiple forms and sensory layers, and the first of them stands out less for its features than for being the official version of the character in the series Arcane. The tier above need not be substantially superior to operate as a new top, and it is enough that the platform reorganizes the regime of signs and couples to it a regime of acquisition that produces the promise of exclusivity as proof.
Prestige is produced by rule, not by necessary material backing.<1>p. 299</1>

A contemporary example of how signs of delivery can be artificially reordered to sustain value, commensurability and prestige is the creation of the Exalted tier and of the acquisition space called Sanctum, presented as a shelf “above” the traditional top of the catalog.<1>p. 298</1>
After the controversy involving Soul Fighter Samira and the public discussion about the elasticity of the meaning of Ultimate, the platform does not “correct” the semantics of the top.<1>p. 298</1>

The first Exalted skin, Arcane Fractured Jinx, is described as a package with multiple forms, with “two models” distributed across “three forms”, with narrative-oriented VFX and form-specific voiceover, switchable in match by a dedicated mechanism <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024g)</2>.<3>p. 299-300</3>

The effect becomes even sharper when one observes that the material grammar presented as Exalted largely recapitulates the grammar historically associated with the top of the catalog as Ultimate, based on transformation, multiple forms, sensory layers and in-game reactivity.<1>p. 299</1>

In general terms, what makes the forms presented by the skin stand out is not the features, but the fact that it is the official skin of the character that portrays her in her “alternate versions” as portrayed in the series Arcane.<1>p. 300</1>

In terms of symbolic functioning, the tier “above” need not be substantially superior to the previous top to operate as a new top. It is enough that the platform reorganizes the regime of signs and assigns to it a category as a marker of luxury linked to mostly aesthetic-cultural elements, while coupling it to a regime of acquisition that produces the promise of exclusivity as proof.<1>p. 300</1>

The price makes the shift visible. An Ultimate skin costs 3,250 RP, the game's paid currency, while the Exalted one is obtained through draws of 400 RP each, guaranteed only on the eightieth, which sets a ceiling of 32,000 RP, about 9.85 times more. Converted into reais, in typical purchase arrangements, the amounts are illustrative and do not fix a single price across all possible combinations. The jump is illustrative evidence that luxury, in this arrangement, is produced mainly by signs and by administered access. The observation matters for reading the promise, because in traditional markets the qualification of luxury presupposes a recognizable backing of superiority capable of sustaining the implicit expectation of quality and of distinction proportional to the price.

In the same official material, Riot defines RP as a premium currency “only obtainable through direct purchase in the store [...]”, that is, obtained by direct purchase <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025o)</2>.<3>p. 305</3>

Riot itself records that an Ultimate skin is priced at the level of 3250 RP <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023a)</2>. The Exalted one, in turn, operates by attempts at 400 RP per Ancient Sparks, guaranteed by the eightieth attempt, which sets a ceiling of [80 × 400 RP = 32,000 RP] <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024g; Riot Games, 2025d)</4><5>p. 301</5>
In RP, the maximum value of the Exalted is almost ten times the value of an Ultimate, since [32,000 / 3,250 ≈ 9.85] <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024g; Riot Games, 2023a)</2>.<3>p. 301</3>
Based on the official RP prices for Brazil, the difference becomes even more significant.<1>p. 301</1>

The economic jump thus works as illustrative empirical evidence that luxury, in this arrangement, is produced mainly by signs and by administered access, and not by a necessarily superior material leap. In traditional markets, the qualification of luxury presupposes a recognizable backing of material, technical and symbolic superiority capable of sustaining, before the consumer, the implicit expectation of quality and of distinction proportional to the price.<1>p. 301</1>

The random draw brings the case to the center of this chapter. Gacha, a monetization model based on random draws of virtual items, is the architecture that conditions the enjoyment of desired goods on probabilistic mechanisms and successive draws, often hiding the real cost of acquisition through intermediate currencies and statistical opacity. The same concern appears in loot boxes, in which the utility and value of what is acquired come to depend on internal distribution regimes defined by the platform, and the institutional discussion tends to focus on minimum transparency of the conditions of acquisition, because the supplier concentrates the criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability. Article 20 of Law 15,211/2025<1><2>1</2></1> prohibits loot boxes in games directed at children and adolescents, and the statute serves as evidential data that certain mechanics have already been identified as sensitive. The argument, however, is not the moralization of gacha.

A monetization model based on random draws of virtual items, inspired by capsule vending machines (gashapon). From the perspective of IOCs, it represents an architecture of extraction that conditions the enjoyment of desired goods on probabilistic mechanisms and successive draws, often hiding the real cost of acquisition through intermediate currencies and statistical opacity<1>p. 299</1>

The point of greatest sensitivity appears when monetization relies on random mechanisms for obtaining items, often treated in public debate as loot boxes. In these cases, the utility and value of what is acquired come to depend on internal distribution regimes, availability criteria and limits defined by the platform, besides being linked to signs of scarcity, time windows and rarity regimes that make decisions more dependent on anticipation, urgency and expectation. The institutional discussion then tends to focus on minimum transparency of the conditions of acquisition, protection of vulnerable audiences and control of practices that induce consumption, not by moralization of the sector, but because the supplier concentrates internal criteria on availability, rotation, rarity and, where applicable, probability, under conditions of low external reconstructibility. In this context, Law 15,211/2025 <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]c)</2> offers sufficient normative anchoring to locate the focal point by regulating, from the standpoint of the protection of children and adolescents, the loot box functionality as a mechanism of random acquisition upon payment. The interest of the statute, here, is evidential. Certain mechanics of the ecosystem have already been identified as structurally sensitive and, therefore, open to treatment by criteria.<3>p. 494-495</3>
Art. 20. Loot boxes offered in electronic games directed at children and adolescents are prohibited [...].<1>p. 545</1>

What matters for the argument of the simulacrum is not the moralization of gacha, but the way sign equivalence reorganizes what counts as the top and shifts the proof of delivery from the content to the very consistency of the circuit of signs.<1>p. 299</1>

There are also public indications about balancing and about the suspicion that it is linked to the sale of cosmetics, such as the statement attributed to the designer of the champion Zeri, according to which she would have been weakened to the extreme to avoid dominance in competitive play, and a community analysis that tested, by win rates, whether champions were strengthened when they got a new skin. The first statement is not conclusive proof, and the hypothesis of manipulation associated with the sale of cosmetics need not be treated as an accusation, but as a structural risk. The value of these records lies in what they show about the asymmetry, since the consumer does not, as a rule, have direct means to reconstruct and contest the relation between the promise of enjoyment and the periodic reconfigurations of value. They are indication, not proof, and the whole case serves to show how the promise is read from documents, without allowing any conclusion about the company's conduct.

In coverage of a public statement attributed to the designer responsible for the champion Zeri, it is recorded: “Zeri is one of his greatest failures as a designer” and that she would have been “nerfed into the ground” to avoid dominance in competitive play <1>Fisher</1><2>(Fisher, 2023)</2>. The statement does not, in any instance, stand as conclusive proof.<3>p. 329</3>

Evidence that the suspicion is recurrent and even mobilizes attempts at empirical testing appears in a community analysis that states: “To decide whether a champion got buffed when he gets a new skin, I will take the difference between the winrate 20 days before and 20 days after the patch got released.” <1>GIANTZORG</1><2>(giantZorg, 2019)</2>.<3>p. 329-330</3>

The reference, shows that the very mode of governance by patches, added to the information asymmetry and the absence of a clear duty of substantial equivalence, creates a zone in which suspicions of commercial optimization can thrive, precisely because the consumer does not, as a rule, have direct means to reconstruct and contest, with sufficient verifiability, the relation between the promise of enjoyment and periodic reconfigurations of functional value.<1>p. 330</1>
What does hypercuratorial anticipation add to the offer?

The third description treats time as a governed dimension. Hypercuratorial anticipation is the economic-semiological technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation, deciding what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be elevated to an event. The consumer is kept in continuous readiness for the next cycle, and the platform also sells permanence oriented toward what is to come, converting expectation into an asset and waiting into a material component of enjoyment. The examples come from the same laboratory. Each ranked season was divided into three splits with coupled rewards, and the patch notes mark with date and time the end of one split and the start of the next. The contract, in turn, frames instability as normality by allowing updates and modifications with or without notice.

From here on, the decisive axis becomes time as a governed dimension, because, in regimes of games-as-a-service and continuous digital services, the promise of the IOC no longer behaves as a one-off event of delivery and presents itself as administered continuity, in which value is only sustained by rhythms and milestones that the platform itself organizes.<1>p. 313</1>

The consumer is kept in continuous readiness for “the next cycle”, “the next update”, “the next opportunity”, that is, for the next piece of meaning that reorders the positional value of the ecosystem. The present ceases to be the place of a stabilized delivery and becomes a governed antechamber, in which the promise is renewed by announcements, teasers, roadmaps and “seasons” that function as anticipated delivery on the plane of recognition. Thus, the platform does not sell only the “now”, since it also sells permanence oriented toward what is “to come”, converting expectation into an asset and turning waiting into a material component of enjoyment.<1>p. 314</1>

By announcing and justifying three splits in each ranked season, the company converts the year into smaller units of participation, with rewards and tracks coupled to the completion of these units <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024h)</2>.<3>p. 315</3>

The governance of time gains precision when temporalization is converted into executable dates and times, as happens in the patch notes that announce the end of one split and the start of another with a time stamp and a reference to the local time zone, turning “missing a window” into an administratively delimited event <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024o)</2>.<3>p. 315</3>

The cycle expires on a set day and time and restarts on another, so that the consumer's permanence in the circuit is calibrated by an official regime of deadlines that disciplines return, intensifies urgency and reorganizes the meaning of “being up to date”. This design, in turn, is not without institutional backing, since the contract frames instability as governable normality and recognizes as legitimate the reprogramming of content, access and rhythm by unilateral decision, including through updates and modifications that may occur with or without notice <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 315</3>

For the offer, the consequence is that what is to come ceases to be subjective expectation and becomes part of what is put into circulation, because the platform sells access to sequences, milestones and returns as properties of the good itself, and the object comes to include what the consumer is authorized to expect and to claim as probable continuity. Seasons and roadmaps, which are the public plans for the evolution of the service, passes, events, availability windows, returns and editions make up the devices of this curation, and the promise becomes serialized, with the sequence as the relevant economic unit. Adequacy, then, comes to depend on the good remaining operative in the circuit that gives it value across the cadences. And since it is enough for the future to remain credible and mobilizing, delivery can be continuously postponed without seeming a failure.

Missing a window, failing a milestone or ignoring a cycle is not equivalent to “losing a chance”, but to falling in position in the public regime of comparison that the ecosystem updates in real time.<1>p. 318</1>

What is “to come” ceases to be simple subjective expectation and becomes part of what is put into circulation, because the platform sells the promise of access to sequences, milestones and returns as if they were properties of the good itself, capable of generating socially effective recognition already in the present. In this regime, the IOC is not only what is obtained now, but also what one is authorized to expect and to claim as probable continuity within the ecosystem, which shifts the offer to a model in which the calendar and the presentation of what is to come function as operative components of value.<1>p. 317</1>
“Roadmap” is an expression used in the sense of public (or semi-public) planning of the evolution of the service.<1>p. 314</1>

Seasons and roadmaps structure expectation as a horizon in chapters, converting continuity into meaning and relevance. Passes and progression tracks condition presence and return by tying value to goals and time milestones. Events and collections manufacture belonging and public memory by turning acquisition into situated participation. Availability windows produce temporal scarcity by making access a problem of timing, and not only of price. Returns and relaunches recalibrate prestige by reorganizing what counts as rare, current or “back”. Editions and variations establish an internal scale by grading differences and turning nuances into legible hierarchy.<1>p. 317</1>
With these devices, the promise ceases to be structured as a closed delivery and comes to operate as a serialized promise, in which the sequence becomes the relevant economic unit.<1>p. 317</1>

When the promise is serialized and the sequence constitutes the economic unit, adequacy comes to depend on the good remaining operative in the circuit that gives it value, that is, remaining recognizable, measurable and socially confirmable in the ecosystem across the governed cadences.<1>p. 318</1>

It is not necessary for the future to be fully realized; it is enough that it remain credible and mobilizing. Thus, delivery can be continuously postponed without seeming a failure, because the system keeps the user moving, rewarding adhesion with sufficient signs of continuity and with calibrated temporal scarcity.<1>p. 316</1>

An analogy is a subscription plan for urban transit, whose value lies not only in the card, but in the stability of lines, schedules, transfers and access rules. If the operator, without formally breaching the contract, begins to frequently change schedules and transfers, the consumer still has access to the service, but loses the ability to plan and to foresee consequences, which affects the adequacy of the service as a continuous regime. In platform consumption, anticipation operates in a similar way with calendars, progression milestones and promises of return, and what is to come becomes a sensitive point of verifiability, because shifts in the calendar and in presentation can produce relevant losses without a single, easily identifiable event of nonperformance. The resulting opacity is neither communication noise nor consumer inattention, and the future promise still works as a buffer, taking the place of the present loss.
Consumption ceases to be an event and becomes a regime, in which the continuous governance of the ecosystem is the condition for the effectiveness of extraction.<1>p. 320</1>

In a subscription plan for urban transit, the value lies not only in the card acquired, but in the stability of the system that makes it usable, lines, schedules, transfers and access rules. If the operator, without formally breaching the contract, begins to frequently change schedules, eliminate transfers, reclassify routes and introduce variable validation obstacles, the consumer may continue “having access to the service”, but loses the ability to plan trips and to foresee practical consequences, which affects the adequacy of the service as a continuous regime. In platform consumption, hypercuratorial anticipation operates in a similar way, except with calendars, progression milestones, promises of return and public forms of visibility that are reprogrammed as part of governance.<1>p. 316-317</1>

The practical effect is not only the intensification of desire or urgency, but the compression of the consumer's space of agency, who loses the ability to guide conduct, anticipate consequences and stabilize legitimate expectations about the permanence of what was promised. In this key, what is “to come” becomes a functional component of the immaterial good and a sensitive point of verifiability, because shifts in the calendar and in presentation can produce relevant losses without a single, easily identifiable event of nonperformance.<1>p. 316</1>

Opacity, therefore, is neither communication noise nor lack of attention by the consumer: it is the effect of a reconfigurable architecture in which what is at stake is the maintenance of the conditions that make the promise keep holding over time.<1>p. 319</1>

Anticipation facilitates this exchange because the future promise works as a buffer: the announced future takes the place of the present loss and sustains the feeling of continuity even when restrictions, practical effects, modes of access or performance conditions change in a relevant way.<1>p. 320</1>
When does anticipation cease to be lawful persuasion?

Not all persuasion is unlawful, and the limit for these environments comes from rejecting two symmetrical errors. The first would be to moralize every technique of commercial persuasion, as if all intense advertising, all interface curation or all architecture aimed at conversion were, in itself, unlawful. What the CDC does not admit is that the organization of interest operates through functional opacity, capture of expectation and displacement of what is essential outside the useful field of understanding. The second error would be to see a problem only when the advertising piece, in isolation, contains literal falsity, or when a certain clause, in isolation, is abusive, because under anticipation unlawfulness may lie in the articulation between elements that, seen separately, seem neutral, but that, combined, govern the decision in a structurally asymmetric way.
The market may promote, persuade, dramatize and organize interest.<1>p. 631</1>

This reading prevents two symmetrical errors. The first would be to moralize every technique of commercial persuasion, as if all intense advertising, all interface curation or all architecture aimed at conversion were, in itself, unlawful. That is not the case.<1>p. 631</1>

What the CDC does not admit is that this organization of interest operates through functional opacity, capture of expectation and displacement of what is essential outside the useful field of understanding.<1>p. 631</1>

The second error would be to imagine that a problem exists only when the advertising piece, in isolation, contains literal falsity or when a certain clause, in isolation, is abusive. In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, unlawfulness may lie precisely in the articulation between elements that, seen separately, seem neutral, but that, combined, govern the consumer's decision in a structurally asymmetric way.<1>p. 631-632</1>

Three figures are articulated here. Relevant omission appears when what is essential is deliberately moved outside the decision-making focus, with the supplier emphasizing urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige and relegating to side conditions limitations of use, mutability, parameters of equivalence, possible losses, restricted windows and additional requirements to realize the promise. Misleading advertising manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in enjoyment, either because the platform later downgrades the object, or because the initial promise already concealed the real mode of delivery. Abusive advertising appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, ritualization of acceptance and fragmentation of the relevant conditions. The background of all three is the cycle of promise, intensification and partial delivery, in which the object appears as a rare, limited or virtually guaranteed opportunity, although enjoyment depends on later mechanisms of randomness, internal rebalancing or unilaterally defined equivalences.

Relevant omission appears when what is essential is deliberately moved outside the decision-making focus. The supplier emphasizes urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige, but relegates to side conditions what really defines the substance of enjoyment, such as relevant limitations of use, ordinary mutability of the object, parameters of equivalence, possible losses, restricted windows of use, additional requirements for realizing the promise or specific conditions for maintaining the advertised value. Misleading advertising, in turn, manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in the actual experience of enjoyment, either because the platform later downgrades the object, or because the initial promise already concealed, through ambiguity or architecture of visibility, the real way in which the utility would be delivered. Abusive advertising, finally, appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing their space for deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, ritualization of acceptance and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.<1>p. 631</1>

In these contexts, the platform produces something more sophisticated than simple ordinary commercial persuasion. It builds cycles of promise, intensification and partial delivery, in which the object is presented as a rare, prestigious, limited or virtually guaranteed opportunity, even though actual enjoyment depends on later mechanisms of randomness, mutability, internal rebalancing or unilaterally defined equivalences.<1>p. 631</1>

Advertising, in this construction, returns to its dogmatic place. Drawing on Adalberto Pasqualotto, marketing communication takes part in manufacturing the very disposition to contract, by inflating needs, organizing desires and presenting the path to their satisfaction. On platforms, it often dissolves into hybrid formats, such as recommendation, tutorial, community narrative and influencer content, which reduce the consumer's critical vigilance and blur the perception of the persuasive character of the message. The chapter on semiotic vulnerability deals with advertising deceptiveness as a manifestation of that vulnerability, and here it is enough to note the effect that matters to the regime of the offer, that the abusive arrangement does not depend on a classic ad.
At this point, the role of advertising needs to be brought back to its correct dogmatic place. It is neither external to the contract nor a simple cultural ambience of the market.<1>p. 632</1>

Marketing communication takes part in manufacturing the very disposition to contract by inflating needs, organizing desires and simultaneously presenting the path to their satisfaction, leading the consumer to the culminating moment of adhesion <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 91])</2>.<3>p. 632</3>

Recommendation, entertainment, tutorial, community narrative, demonstration of use, influencer content and advertising piece blend together, reducing the consumer's critical vigilance and blurring the perception of the persuasive status of the message.<1>p. 632</1>
The abusive arrangement, then, does not depend on an explicit banner or a classic ad.<1>p. 632-633</1>
When is the duty to inform considered fulfilled?

The normative starting point is the basic right to adequate and clear information and to protection against misleading and abusive advertising, in Article 6, items III and IV, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, and the requirement of Article 31 of the CDC<3><4>3</4></3> that the offer and presentation ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information about characteristics, price and risks. Claudia Lima Marques reads Article 31 of the CDC<5><6>3</6></5> as a duty to ensure clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product, and observes that the contract does not bind a consumer who was not given the opportunity to learn the content of the obligations, even if duly formalized. Ricardo Morishita Wada adds that the duty to inform requires an active stance from the supplier, who must make the information reach the consumer.

Art. 6. The basic rights of the consumer are: I - the protection of life, health and safety against risks caused by practices in the supply of products and services considered dangerous or harmful; III - adequate and clear information about the different products and services […]; IV - protection against misleading and abusive advertising, coercive or unfair commercial methods, as well as against abusive practices and clauses […];<1>p. 511</1>

Art. 31. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise, conspicuous information in the Portuguese language about their characteristics, qualities, quantity, composition, price, warranty, expiration dates and origin, among other data, as well as about the risks they pose to the health and safety of consumers.<1>p. 601</1>

This is exactly what stands out when interpreting Article 31 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>, stating that the supplier must ensure the consumer “clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product”, including data related to its characteristics, its economic repercussion, health and safety <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 877)</4>. As a reflection of the principle of transparency, the supplier must offer “clear and correct” information about the qualities of the product and the conditions of the contract, drafting the text clearly, so as to “give the consumer the opportunity” to learn the content of the obligations assumed, failing which the contract does not bind them, “even if duly formalized” <5>Marques</5><6>(Marques, 2016, p. 820-821)</6>.<7>p. 618-619</7>

The legal duty requires positive action aimed at the information actually reaching its addressee under conditions of relevant understanding. For this reason, “in the regime of consumer relations, the duty to inform the consumer requires an active stance from the supplier”, who is the one who “must make the information reach the consumer” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</2>.<3>p. 619</3>

In platform ecosystems, the duty is not measured in quantitative terms, and the accumulation of texts, links, notices, policies and explanatory windows does not, in itself, satisfy the requirement of adequate information, and may even produce merely apparent transparency. The parameter has a double function. To inform, in a legally relevant sense, is to make the essential elements of enjoyment intelligible at the moment the decision is formed and, at the same time, to preserve minimum conditions for later reconstructing what was promised, what was shown and what was altered. The second function links the duty to inform to open auditability, which is an internal development of that duty and has its own chapter.
To inform is not merely to make content available.<1>p. 722</1>

In platform ecosystems, the duty to inform cannot be understood in merely quantitative terms. The simple accumulation of texts, links, notices, policies, terms and explanatory windows does not, in itself, satisfy the requirement of adequate information. In many cases, this accumulation operates precisely in the opposite direction, producing an environment of merely apparent transparency, in which the proliferation of statements replaces the legibility of what actually matters for deciding, adhering, remaining or contesting.<1>p. 722</1>

To inform, in a legally relevant sense, is to make the essential elements of enjoyment intelligible at the moment the consumer's decision is formed and, at the same time, to preserve minimum conditions for later reconstruction of what was promised, what was shown and what was altered. Adequate information, therefore, is not measured by the volume of what was published, but by its aptitude to guide conduct and allow institutional verification.<1>p. 722</1>

The problem then ceases to be the presence or absence of isolated data and comes to lie in the relation between promise, mode of presentation, real conditions of use and the institutional possibility of auditing the informational trajectory of the bond.<1>p. 723</1>

Inadequacy can take three forms. There is excess when textual overload makes it impracticable to distinguish the essential from the accessory, dispersion when the relevant elements are scattered across documents, screens and paths without integration, and flow architecture when the experience is designed to highlight the attractive and move the onerous, the contingent or the restrictive to zones of low visibility. The result is functional opacity produced by design, a specific form of informational nonperformance in which the appearance of openness replaces the legibility of the regime of enjoyment. Performative transparency, which the chapter on semiotic vulnerability examines, has the same structure of excess, dispersion and defective ranking of the essential. The resulting test has two questions, whether the datum was made accessible, comprehensible and relevant at the moment it could influence the legitimate formation of expectation or the consumer's reaction, and whether the arrangement preserves minimum trails to reconstitute the link between offer, presentation, modulation of enjoyment and alteration of content. In objects of high cognitive complexity, including those whose utility involves guidance, filtering or prioritization, breach can occur without literal falsity and without absolute silence.

Informational inadequacy can thus take the form of excess, dispersion and flow architecture. Excess, when textual overload makes it impracticable to distinguish the essential from the accessory. Dispersion, when the relevant elements of the bond are scattered across multiple documents, screens and paths without sufficient integration. Flow architecture, when the informational experience is designed to highlight the attractive, simplify the favorable and move the onerous, the contingent or the restrictive to zones of low visibility, lower salience or improbable reading.<1>p. 722-723</1>

This is functional opacity produced by design, that is, a specific form of informational nonperformance in which the appearance of openness replaces the actual legibility of the regime of enjoyment.<1>p. 723</1>

The legally relevant question is no longer whether a given datum was somewhere in the supplier's documentary ecosystem. It becomes whether this datum was made accessible, comprehensible and relevant at the moment it could influence the legitimate formation of expectation or the consumer's reaction. Likewise, in case of later dispute, what matters is whether the informational arrangement preserves minimum trails that allow reconstituting the link between offer, presentation of the environment, modulation of enjoyment and alteration of the content of the relationship.<1>p. 723</1>

This formulation absorbs an important consequence for immaterial objects of consumption of high cognitive complexity, including those in which the very utility of the object involves guidance, filtering, prioritization or informational support. In these contexts, breach of the duty can occur without any literal falsity and without any absolute silence.<1>p. 723</1>

Under hypercuratorial anticipation, if the promotional architecture creates intensity and scarcity to hasten the decision, the duty to inform needs to work as a counterweight to this acceleration, and not as a bureaucratic ritual completed in background documents, so that the essential content must come in a comparable, ranked, conspicuous and timely way. In IOCs, the essential includes price, total cost, relevant restrictions, ordinary mutability of the object, criteria of equivalence, potential loss of items, refund conditions, cases of suspension, limits of use and substantial impacts of updates. Article 54, paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC provides the form, by requiring that adhesion contracts be drafted in clear terms and in conspicuous and legible characters, and that clauses limiting rights be highlighted and allow immediate and easy understanding.

It is not enough for text to exist. The essential content must be presented in a comparable, ranked, conspicuous and timely way. If the promotional architecture of the environment creates intensity and scarcity to hasten the decision, the duty to inform needs to work as a counterweight to this acceleration, and not as a bureaucratic ritual completed in background documents.<1>p. 633</1>

In practical terms, this means that the informational regime must clearly expose, at the decision point, the elements that structure the choice: price, total cost, relevant restrictions, ordinary mutability of the object, criteria of equivalence, potential loss of items, refund conditions, cases of suspension, limits of use and substantial impacts of updates.<1>p. 621</1>

This is precisely what Article 54, under paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC makes explicit. Adhesion contracts must be drafted in clear terms, in conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding, and clauses limiting rights must be drafted with emphasis, allowing immediate and easy understanding.<1>p. 621</1>
When does promotional communication become part of the offer?

In ecosystems in which enjoyment is prepared by cycles of anticipation, advertising and the offer cannot be treated as an external, ornamental or legally neutral layer. In many of these objects, the offer is not limited to the final purchase statement and is built progressively through an economy of signs that precedes enjoyment and conditions how the consumer interprets what is acquired. Teasers, which are short pieces of advance communication, storefronts, previews, countdowns, suggestions of rarity, insinuated equivalences and promises of prestige, belonging or performance make up the program of the offer insofar as they take part in forming legitimate expectation. The basic rule is in Article 30 of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>, under which all sufficiently precise information or advertising binds the supplier and becomes part of the contract. This holds with special force when the utility is mediated by interface, visual presentation and promises of progression, and the offer does not disappear after adhesion. Rizzatto Nunes recognizes that the offer can arise from the mere presentation of the product in the storefront, which supports reading the digital storefront as a binding offer.

In ecosystems in which enjoyment is preceded, prepared and guided by continuous cycles of anticipation, advertising and the offer cannot be treated as an external, ornamental or legally neutral layer of consumption.<1>p. 724</1>

In many immaterial objects of consumption, what is acquired is not only a functional utility described in a static way, but an experience previously framed by signs, promises, narratives of distinction, projections of value and expectations administered by the supplier itself. The offer, in these cases, is not limited to the final purchase statement. It is built progressively through an economy of signs that precedes enjoyment, organizes its horizon of meaning and conditions how the consumer interprets what is being acquired.<1>p. 724</1>
They designate short pieces of advance communication, usually fragmentary or enigmatic, aimed at arousing curiosity and building expectation around future launches or updates.<1>p. 314</1>

Teasers, storefronts, promotional events, announcement cycles, previews, countdowns, suggestions of rarity, insinuated equivalences, promises of prestige, belonging or performance and narrative models of scarcity do not operate, in these environments, as mere accessory persuasion. They make up the program of the offer insofar as they take part in forming legitimate expectation and in determining the value attributed to the object.<1>p. 724</1>

“Art. 30. All sufficiently precise information or advertising, conveyed by any form or means of communication regarding products and services offered or presented, binds the supplier that conveys it or makes use of it and becomes part of the contract that may be entered into.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 562</3>

The offer also does not disappear after adhesion. In long-term relationships, information, advertising and contractual performance remain connected, so that the promised content continues to function as a parameter of adequacy of the performance. All sufficiently precise information becomes part of the contract and binds the supplier, and this holds with special force when the utility consumed is mediated by interface, visual presentation, promises of progression and digital externalization of the experience.<1>p. 562</1>

Moreover, when interpreting Article 30 [...] the author recognizes that the offer can arise from the mere presentation of the product in the storefront <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 312])</2>, which supports reading the digital storefront as a binding offer.<3>p. 433</3>

The material reading makes it possible to recognize deceptiveness that the logic of frontal falsity does not capture, because inducement into error can result from constructed ambiguity, from strategically distributed relevant omission or from a mismatch between the overall meaning of the promise and the real conditions of enjoyment under administered mutability. Advertising can suggest stability where there is structural precariousness, rarity where there is programmed artificiality and continuity where there is intense mutability. Hypercuratorial anticipation, therefore, is part of the very legal economy of the offer, especially when the utility has a symbolic, relational or reputational dimension, because in these cases use value and meaning value intertwine and the consumer also acquires insertion into a network of distinction shaped by the supplier's communication.
Advertising does not externally surround the object; it helps produce it as an expectation of performance, distinction, utility or permanence.<1>p. 633</1>
