Hypercuratorial anticipation thus is part of the very legal economy of the offer.<1>p. 725</1>

This becomes even more evident in environments in which the utility consumed has a relevant symbolic, relational or reputational dimension. In such cases, use value and meaning value intertwine. The consumer acquires not only access or functionality, but also insertion into a network of distinction, recognition, belonging or identity projection previously shaped by the supplier's communication.<1>p. 725</1>

Control falls on three objects, what was promised as value and as function, what was concealed as cost, limitation or condition of precariousness, and the correspondence between this semiotic frame and real enjoyment. The condition for application is that promotional communication takes part in determining what the consumer legitimately understands they are acquiring, because then it is incorporated into the normative field of the offer and becomes subject to control for deceptiveness, ambiguity or relevant omission. The examination needs to capture the overall regime of signification, since the promise may emerge from elements merely suggested by salience, timing, symbolic association or strategic repetition, and the mismatch between promise and delivery may appear as frustration of the symbolic or relational position presented as the core of the acquisition. Advertising thus has a function of semiotic hygiene of the offer, and communication that produces ambiguity or obscures what is onerous may take part in the abusive teleology of the ecosystem, especially when it is articulated with mutability, artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency or deliberate opacity.

Control of the offer must fall on what was promised as value and as function, on what was concealed as cost, limitation or condition of precariousness, and on the correspondence between this semiotic frame and the real enjoyment made available to the consumer.<1>p. 725</1>

Whenever promotional communication takes part in determining what the consumer legitimately understands they are acquiring, it is incorporated into the normative field of the offer and becomes subject to control for deceptiveness, ambiguity or relevant omission.<1>p. 725</1>

The legally relevant promise is not always concentrated in a single statement. Often, it emerges from the articulation between multiple elements of the communicational environment, some explicit, others insinuated, others merely suggested by salience, timing, symbolic association or strategic repetition. Control must, therefore, capture the overall regime of signification produced by the supplier. This requirement is particularly important in immaterial objects of consumption whose enjoyment depends on visibility, reputation, collective recognition or insertion in an ecosystem of symbolic value. In them, the mismatch between promise and delivery may not manifest itself as an evident technical defect, but as relevant frustration of the symbolic or relational position presented as part of the core of the acquisition. For this reason too, advertising takes on a function of semiotic hygiene of the offer.<1>p. 725-726</1>

When communication is designed to produce ambiguity, artificially highlight the favorable, obscure the onerous or move the essential to zones of low visibility, it ceases to be a mere persuasive frame and becomes part of the very program of supply. In this condition, it may take part not only in forming inadequate expectation, but in the very abusive teleology of the ecosystem, especially when it is articulated with later mechanisms of mutability, artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency or deliberate opacity.<1>p. 726</1>
Is it enough to say it was in the terms and that the consumer accepted?

The supplier's standard defense is that everything was in the contract and that the consumer agreed. But the formula confuses formal existence with material fulfillment of the duty, because the contract may contain a nominal reference to the risk, alteration or limitation and still fail to inform adequately, if the organization of the communicational whole produces noise, minimizes the impact of the datum or makes its practical connection with the decision unfeasible. The decisive point is not to prove that the text was there, but to assess whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms. Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1> provides the sanction, since contracts do not bind the consumer if they were not given the opportunity to learn the content in advance or if they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope, and Claudia Lima Marques links this sanction to the presumption of bad faith of the supplier who drafted the contract.

Wherever there is excess without guidance, abundance without hierarchy, documentation without legibility or transparency without reconstructibility, there will be no true fulfillment of the duty.<1>p. 724</1>

The centrality of verifiable adequacy also prevents the supplier's standard defense from being satisfied with the claim that “everything was in the contract”. This formula confuses formal existence with material fulfillment of the duty. In environments of high informational complexity, the contract may even contain a nominal reference to the disputed risk, alteration or limitation, but still fail to inform adequately if the organization of the communicational whole produces noise, minimizes the impact of the relevant datum or makes its practical connection with the consumer's decision unfeasible.<1>p. 723</1>
The decisive point, therefore, is not to prove that “the text was there”, but to assess whether the legally relevant meaning was knowable in real terms.<1>p. 601</1>

Art. 46. Contracts governing consumer relations shall not bind consumers if they are not given the opportunity to learn their content in advance, or if the respective instruments are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope.<1>p. 601</1>

Breach of the duty of clear drafting finds its sanction in Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1>, according to which contracts do not bind the consumer if they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope, a sanction that originates in the "presumption of bad faith of the supplier who drafted the contract" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 902-903)</4>.<5>p. 605</5>

As for acceptance, there is a communicational continuum in which the platform produces expectation, guides the reading of the object, administers the pace of the decision and only then stabilizes acceptance in documentary forms that often do not reflect, with the same emphasis, the promise that triggered the bond. Final acceptance does not erase the environment that prepared it, because this pre-contractual environment already takes part in the material constitution of consent. On interpretation, Claudia Lima Marques maintains that the interpreter must observe not only the rule of Article 47 of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1>, but all the norms of the Code, because the content of the contract to be interpreted includes the entire prior context that constitutes the offer, such as advertising, brochures and information. And the more precise and guiding the advertising, the greater its binding force, which prevents the supplier from capturing trust in the pre-contractual phase and then trying to dehydrate it in the final text of the contract or in mutable internal rules.

Instead of a clean, compartmentalized sequence between ad, information and contracting, what exists is a communicational continuum in which the platform produces expectation, guides the reading of the object, administers the pace of the decision and only then stabilizes acceptance in documentary forms that often do not reflect, with the same emphasis, the promise that triggered the bond. This means that abusiveness cannot be located only in the final statement, because the pre-contractual environment itself already takes part in the material constitution of consent.<1>p. 632</1>

The interpreter of the consumer contract must observe not only the rule of Article 47 of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1>, but all the norms of the Code that establish rights and duties of consumer and supplier, so that “the content of the contract to be interpreted is not only that ‘placed’ in clauses pre-drafted unilaterally by the supplier, but also the entire prior context that constitutes the offer”, such as advertising, brochures, information and commercial practices <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1015)</4>.<5>p. 634</5>

The more precise, eloquent and guiding the advertising, the greater its aptitude to generate legitimate expectation and, therefore, the greater also its binding force. This is decisive because it prevents the old maneuver of capturing trust in the pre-contractual phase and then trying to dehydrate it in the final text of the contract or in mutable internal rules.<1>p. 627-628</1>
What can the lawyer demonstrate and request?

The methodological consequence is that the analysis must consider the communicational and decision-making arrangement as a whole, and not isolated fragments of its formal expression. Hence the questions that fall to the jurist, about how the expectation was produced, at what moment the relevant conditions were revealed, with what prominence they appeared, what the actual sequence between promise and acceptance was and whether the consumer had real means to understand and compare what was offered. The material for these questions is concrete, since open auditability requires the minimum preservation of screens, flows, messages, promotional pieces, interface changes and decision trails, and proof of informational adequacy depends on documentation of the purchase flow, the confirmation screens, the notices of alteration and the visual location of the limitations. It is not enough for the platform to claim generically that it informed, because it must be able to demonstrate how, when and with what prominence it informed.

The most important methodological consequence of the item is this: consumer law analysis must consider the communicational and decision-making arrangement as a whole, and not only isolated fragments of its formal expression. The jurist needs to ask how the expectation was produced, at what moment the relevant conditions were revealed, with what prominence they appeared, what the actual sequence between promise and acceptance was, and whether the consumer had real means to understand and compare what was offered. This places choice architecture back within the field of the CDC without technological mysticism and without creating a parallel law of platforms.<1>p. 633-634</1>

With this shift, two operators are prepared. The first is open auditability, because, if abusiveness can lie in the communicational regime of supply, this regime must be institutionally reconstructible, with minimum preservation of screens, flows, messages, promotional pieces, interface changes and decision trails. The second is functional value equivalence, because the expectation produced by hypercuratorial anticipation cannot be discarded as promotional smoke when it served precisely to induce the acquisition and shape the understanding of the object.<1>p. 634</1>

In IOCs, proof of informational adequacy depends on minimum documentation of the purchase flow, the confirmation screens, the notices of alteration, the form of presentation of equivalences and the visual location of the relevant limitations. It is not enough for the platform to claim generically that it informed. It must be able to demonstrate how it informed, when it informed and with what prominence it informed.<1>p. 623</1>

In advertising, Article 38 of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1> places the burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication on whoever sponsors it, and the provision ensures that the consumer does not have to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the actual regime of enjoyment. The expectation created by anticipation cannot be discarded as promotional smoke when it served to induce the acquisition, and if the platform promises a curated experience of value, rarity or performance and then downgrades it under opaque criteria, the frustration is not a mere annoyance and may be a relevant inadequacy of governed enjoyment itself. For refusal to honor the offer, presentation or advertising, Article 35 of the CDC<3><4>8</4></3> allows the consumer to demand specific performance, accept an equivalent performance or rescind the contract with losses and damages, and the chapter on remedies deals with the order among these options.

It is precisely for this reason that Article 38 of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1>, here, proves so important. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication falls on whoever sponsors it.<3>p. 627</3>
In IOCs, this provision prevents the consumer from having to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the actual regime of enjoyment.<1>p. 627</1>

If the supplier of products or services refuses to honor the offer, presentation or advertising, the consumer may, alternatively and at their free choice: I - demand specific performance of the obligation […]; II - accept another equivalent product or provision of service; III - rescind the contract […], and to losses and damages.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 540</3>
Can advertising still persuade?

The first limit is that of persuasion. Economic activity has its own persuasive function, and control of the offer does not work as abstract repression of advertising, but as control of the promise in environments of governed enjoyment. The second is that of relevance. Informational adequacy is assessed by the elements that relevantly condition the formation of expectation, the preservation of enjoyment and the possibility of contestation, and there is a materially controllable offer wherever prior communication relevantly shapes the reading of the object, the perception of value and adhesion. The third is that of the symbolic. The contribution of the simulacrum does not lie in treating consumption as illusion, and the problem does not lie in desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object. The fourth is that of possibilities. The consequences of anticipation come with a modal, since unlawfulness may lie in the articulation and frustration may be a relevant inadequacy, so that a calendar, an event or a random draw does not become abusive merely by existing.

This is not a matter of denying the persuasive function proper to economic activity, but of recognizing that, in platform-governed ecosystems, persuasion can turn into a technique of structural shaping of expectation and, therefore, must be subject to the limits of the consumer protection regime.<1>p. 725</1>

Wherever prior communication relevantly shapes the reading of the object, becomes part of the perception of its value and conditions the consumer's adhesion, there will be an offer in a materially controllable sense. And wherever this management of meaning operates to produce relevant ambiguity, shift cognitive costs, conceal precariousness or artificially inflate perceived utility, there will be sufficient grounds for the application of the protective regime, not as abstract repression of advertising, but as control of the promise in environments of governed enjoyment.<1>p. 726</1>

Informational adequacy must be assessed by the capacity of the communicational arrangement to make visible and comprehensible the elements that relevantly condition the formation of expectation, the preservation of enjoyment and the possibility of contestation.<1>p. 724</1>
The problem is not desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object.<1>p. 629</1>

The law of the platform
Why does the contract not describe the power the platform exercises?

When the enjoyment of an Immaterial Object of Consumption depends on signs, visibility and equivalences that exist only while the environment maintains them, the acquisition comes to depend on an ecosystem that provides intelligibility, comparison and the possibility of sanction and that defines, in practice, access, permanence and hierarchies. The core of the problem is institutional. The platform does not merely intermediate a bilateral relationship between supplier and acquirer, because it organizes at the same time the normative content of the environment and the means of enforcing it.

Up to this point, enjoyment has appeared as a position sustained by signs, visibility and equivalences that exist only while the environment keeps them operative. In this condition, the acquisition depends on an ecosystem that provides intelligibility, commensurability and the possibility of sanction, while at the same time defining, in practice, access, permanence and hierarchies. For this reason, the description of the IOC, when it seeks to support legal control, cannot remain confined to the vocabulary of price or to the psychological repertoire of preference. The core is institutional, because the platform administers the conditions of enjoyment and, by this route, stabilizes value as a recognizable position, even when the relevant experience is reconfigured over time.<1>p. 330</1>

What matters is identifying which operations make up this occupation, what effects it produces on the position of enjoyment and what asymmetries it installs between consumer and administrator of the ecosystem, so as to allow evaluation of conduct, duties and restoration without depending on impressionistic readings of the conflict. For this, it is necessary to recognize that, in the IOC regime, the platform does not merely intermediate a bilateral relationship between supplier and acquirer. It organizes, simultaneously, the normative content of the environment and the mechanisms of its enforcement.<1>p. 331</1>

This power breaks down into four operations. The platform defines and updates rules of access and permanence, administers visibility and reputation through metrics and rankings, continuously curates what appears, disappears and returns and applies sanctions that degrade the symbolic position and interrupt enjoyment, in a key close to a functional and identity dispossession. The description of these powers does not require assuming subjective intent, because control is exercised through architecture and information, with design decisions, moderation parameters and access rules that operate as silent infrastructure. The consumer faces not just a contract, but an integrated set of devices that keep the actual operating criteria opaque.

First, it defines and updates internal rules that structure access and permanence, establishing permissions, incentives and punishments through moderation, functional restrictions or exclusions. Second, it administers visibility and reputation as economically relevant dimensions, through metrics, rankings, signs of prestige and instruments of public comparison that produce hierarchies and modulate the experience. Third, it exercises continuous curation of what appears, what disappears and what returns, controlling the horizon of expectation and reorganizing the temporality of consumption. Finally, it applies sanctions and restrictions with effects that go beyond the loss of a one-off utility, degrading symbolic position, interrupting continuity of enjoyment and reconfiguring the economic meaning of the IOC, in a key close to functional and identity dispossession.<1>p. 331</1>

The description of these powers does not require the assumption of subjective intent, because what is at stake is a mode of functioning in which control is exercised through architecture and through information.<1>p. 331</1>

In digital environments, relevant normativity does not manifest itself only as an explicit command, but as a configuration of choices, rhythms, frictions and incentives that makes certain conduct more probable and other conduct more costly, while defining the criteria by which the environment itself will recognize, reward or sanction the user. This governance is carried out through design decisions, moderation parameters, recommendation patterns and access rules that operate as silent infrastructure, so that coercion need not present itself as frontal prohibition to produce obedience, predictability and conformity.<1>p. 331-332</1>

The result is that the consumer faces not just a contract, but an integrated set of devices that guide the experience and stabilize hierarchies, while keeping the actual operating criteria opaque, creating a structural asymmetry between those who live the ecosystem and those who control the variables that define its conditions of legibility, permanence and value.<1>p. 332</1>

Hence the formula that the platform occupies the place of the collectivity without authorization, which states a descriptive problem, and not a generic political judgment. Without authorization means that the platform exercises functions of social ordering without a public mandate and without submitting, to an equivalent extent, to requirements of institutional reciprocity, and what is lacking is not formal delegation, but counterweights of legitimacy.

The relevant absence is not that of formal delegation, but of minimum guarantees that function as counterweights of legitimacy, such as intelligible publicity of criteria, the possibility of verification, decision-making coherence, accessible reasoning and effective avenues of contestation.<1>p. 332</1>

The formula according to which the platform “occupies the place of the collectivity without authorization” is treated as a descriptive problem to be stabilized in verifiable institutional terms, failing which it remains an intuition without legal consequence.<1>p. 331</1>

It is in this strict sense that the expression “without authorization” must be understood, not as a generic political judgment, but as the finding that the platform exercises functions of social ordering without holding a public mandate and without submitting, to an equivalent extent, to requirements of institutional reciprocity.<1>p. 332</1>

For consumer law, the consequence is an adjustment of lens, and not a rhetorical expansion of protection. If the IOC exists as a position of governed enjoyment, the contract is not an exhaustive declaration of its content, and the task is no longer just to check isolated abusive clauses but to understand that the environment itself produces vulnerability, with duties proportional to the power exercised. The resulting key is that of the platform as a private power with practical normativity, which takes the debate out of the simplifying opposition between contractual freedom and state intervention.

Once this structure is recognized, the consequence for consumer law cannot be formulated as a simple rhetorical expansion of protection, but as an adjustment of lens capable of reaching the way in which the offer is carried out in practice. If the IOC exists as a position of governed enjoyment and if value depends on internal criteria of recognition, protection cannot be content with reading the contract as an exhaustive declaration of content, because the actual shaping of the object is produced by rules, architecture and continued operations that exceed the documentary form and that can unilaterally alter the continuity of supply.<1>p. 332</1>

The question, therefore, is not only to check isolated abusive clauses, but to understand that the environment itself functions as a mechanism for producing vulnerability, which makes duties proportional to the power exercised relevant.<1>p. 332</1>

The expected result is to fix a conceptual key according to which the platform, in the IOC regime, operates as a private power with practical normativity, because it administers not only conditions of exchange, but conditions of enjoyment and recognition in a governed environment. This key shifts the debate from the simplifying opposition between contractual freedom and state intervention to a plane in which internal rules, design, curation and enforcement constitute the economic object itself and distribute risks of loss, exclusion and degradation of value.<1>p. 333</1>

The authors have delimited functions. Julie E. Cohen describes the power that stabilizes when information and architecture become practical governance, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis provide the matrix of legal reconstruction in the face of technical change, Byung-Chul Han reads adhesion and self-adjustment as a structural effect, and not as individual fragility, and Eros Grau blocks both the liberal neutralization of private normativity and its hasty transposition into the category of the State.

With Julie E. Cohen <1>(2012; 2019)</1>, the specific form of power that stabilizes when information and architecture become means of practical governance is delimited, making it possible to treat choices, standards and infrastructures as normative mechanisms that organize conduct and distribute possibilities. Warren and Brandeis <2>([201-?])</2> are mobilized as a methodological matrix of legal reconstruction in the face of technical changes that reconfigure exposure and vulnerability, indicating that changes in the material conditions of social life require reinterpretation of categories without resorting to moralization of the phenomenon.<3>p. 333</3>

Byung-Chul Han <1>(2015; 2017)</1> is used as a lens to describe adhesion and self-adjustment through performance, comparison and expectation, qualifying subjection as a structural effect of incentives and of the management of symbolic risk, instead of attributing it to individual fragilities. Eros Grau <2>(2008)</2> provides the conceptual lock to avoid both the liberal neutralization of private normativity and its hasty transposition into the category of the State, making it possible to describe it as presupposed law endowed with collective effects and, therefore, demanding criteria of control compatible with its density.<3>p. 333</3>
How does the platform govern without needing to give orders?

The first piece is governance by architecture, in which design and infrastructure decisions work as the practical grammar of the environment and configure the consumer's field of action before any command. Defaults, which are the options already set when the user arrives, define where the experience begins, selective frictions make deviations more costly, access windows and expirations produce urgency and scarcity, and visibility becomes economic language. The platform does not merely present options, because it distributes probabilities and costs and decides which signs are enough to produce prestige, belonging or sanction.

Governance by architecture, for this scope, designates the way in which design and infrastructure decisions operate as the practical grammar of the environment, configuring the consumer's field of action before any explicit command.<1>p. 336</1>

Defaults organize the user's entry and stabilize tracks of enjoyment, because they determine where the experience “begins” and which choices appear as natural, while selective frictions make deviations more costly, multiply steps, impose waits or require specific skills to reach results outside the script. Added to this is the administration of time as a structural operator of the field of action, since access windows, events, expirations, returns and update rhythms convert the availability of content into a practical condition of permanence, producing urgency and functional scarcity through calendar and recurrence. Finally, visibility functions as the economic language of the ecosystem, since rankings, metrics and signs of prestige make public comparison continuous and make the user's position continuously legible and rankable.<1>p. 341</1>

Access flows, rhythms of use and visibility criteria organize what will be found, compared and recognized as value. In this regime, the platform does not merely present options. It also distributes probabilities and costs, decides where the user enters by default and which signs will be enough to produce prestige, belonging or sanction.<1>p. 336</1>

Drawing on Cohen, protocols and standards are practical means of ordering, with dense normative effects that are not to be confused with formal law or state authority, and standardization, as the author notes, can shift normative authority to the standard itself. Ana Flávia Merino Lesnovski, whose doctoral research in Social Communication deals with games and interactive narrative, without having legal regulation as its object, adds the experience of controlled freedom, in which the user acts in relation to a structure that precedes and conditions them. She also shows that rewards and punishments lead whoever interacts back to the intended path. Choice does not disappear, but arrives shaped by paths, hierarchies of visibility and regimes of consequence.

The operational description of governance by architecture requires treating protocols, standards and informational devices as practical means of ordering, because the platform defines the space in which activities become possible and legible.<1>p. 336</1>

When informational protocols and networked devices reshape spaces and practices, they encode dependencies and habits of behavior and stabilize paths as if they were natural <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 19])</2>. With this, architecture and information operate as an infrastructure of everyday governance, creating tracks of conduct and silently limiting alternatives, without this being confused with formal law or state authority, but still with normative effects dense enough to reorganize the possibilities of acting within the ecosystem.<3>p. 336</3>

Standards and protocols do not serve only interoperability, since they organize practical hierarchies and define forms of conformity. For this reason, standardization can shift normative authority to the standard itself and, simultaneously, open opportunities for the exercise of economic and political power <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 218)</2>.<3>p. 339</3>

The contribution of Ana Flávia Merino Lesnovski, expressed in her doctoral thesis entitled Uma experiência paradigmática: jogos e tensões no encontro entre a narrativa e a interatividade em forma audiovisual e eletrônica, defended before the Graduate Program in Social Communication at PUC-RS in 2014, is useful here not because her object is the regulation of platforms in a legal key, but because her thesis offers a particularly fertile conceptual grammar for understanding interactive experiences structured by technical control.<1>p. 337</1>

In examining interactive narratives and games, Lesnovski observes that this type of experience is organized by permanent tensions between choice and control, illusion and simulation, action and identity, culminating in the production of an “experience of controlled freedom”, in which the user's action always occurs in relation to a structure that precedes and conditions it <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7)</2>.<3>p. 336</3>

In a similar direction, in dealing with systems of reward and punishment, Lesnovski shows that they do not operate only as episodic reactions to isolated conduct, but as forms of the system's control over free and potentially deviant actions, keeping the experience in flow, avoiding aporias and leading whoever interacts back to the structurally intended path <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 79-80)</2>.<3>p. 337</3>

Freedom of choice, in this framework, does not disappear, but appears already shaped by paths, responses, hierarchies of visibility and regimes of consequence that silently delimit what can be done, found, recognized and maintained.<1>p. 336-337</1>

The second piece is informational domination, and the jurist needs to be careful with the word. The information in question is not that of the duty to inform under the Consumer Protection Code, which deals with price, characteristics, risks, conditions and limitations of supply. Informational domination is the power that arises from concentrated control of the variables that make the experience measurable, classifiable and sanctionable, such as data, metrics, ranking criteria, recommendation parameters and activity records. For this reason the asymmetry can persist even with formal openings of information, since the consumer perceives the interface and its effects, while the platform controls the criteria of recognition.
The core is not concealment of clauses or price, but administration of the categories and signs by which enjoyment will be recognized and converted into value.<1>p. 340</1>
